It's the first week of July. Nomsa goes to buy electricity, the same five hundred rand she spends every month. But this time, she gets fewer units. The price went up again on the first of July.

She didn't use more. She didn't do anything wrong. Her electricity just costs more. Again. And she's not imagining it.

And it's not just this year. Since 2007, electricity prices in South Africa have gone up by about nine hundred percent. Over the same time, prices in general went up by about a hundred and fifty percent.

So how did Eskom, the company that makes most of our electricity, end up so deep in debt, that the government had to step in with two hundred and fifty-four billion rand? And what does it cost you, every month?

Here's the lesson up front: electricity will keep getting more expensive, faster than most things you buy. So it needs its own line in your budget, with a raise every year. By the end of this video, you'll see why, and exactly how to plan for it. Let's start from zero.

Eskom was set up in 1923, to supply electricity to the whole country. Over the decades, it built big coal power stations, mostly in Mpumalanga, close to the coal mines.

But the country grew, and Eskom didn't build fast enough. In 2007, the lights started going out. Load shedding had begun.

So Eskom started building two giant coal power stations: Medupi and Kusile, each about four thousand eight hundred megawatts. They were supposed to be finished years ago.

They didn't. Kusile was budgeted at about eighty billion rand. It ended up costing more than one hundred and sixty billion, and finished more than eleven years late. Its last unit only started running in September 2025. Together, the two stations went more than three hundred billion rand over budget.

Every one of those rand had to come from somewhere. Eskom borrowed it. And borrowed money has to be paid back, with interest.

Now the debt piled up. Eskom was paying billions in interest every year, while its old power stations kept breaking down.

And 2023 was the worst year of all. South Africa had close to seven thousand hours of load shedding. Shops ran generators. Factories cut shifts. Families cooked by candlelight.

That same year, Parliament passed the Eskom Debt Relief Act. The government would give Eskom up to two hundred and fifty-four billion rand over three years, to help pay its debt. That's taxpayers' money. Your money.

And there was another hole. Many municipalities buy electricity from Eskom, sell it to you, and then don't pay Eskom in full. By March 2026, municipalities owed Eskom one hundred and eleven point six billion rand. That's up almost eighteen percent in one year.

So when you pay your municipality for electricity, part of that money is supposed to reach Eskom. In too many towns, it doesn't.

So where does Eskom stand today? The news is better than it's been in years.

Load shedding has mostly stopped. In its last financial year, to March 2026, Eskom had just four days of load shedding, twenty-six hours in total. Its power stations are working more reliably: they were available about sixty-five percent of the time, up from about sixty-one, though still short of Eskom's own target of seventy.

And Eskom made a profit: thirty point three billion rand, more than double the year before. That's its second profit in a row, after eight years of losses. Its net debt fell to three hundred and thirteen billion rand.

But there's a new problem. Eskom is selling less electricity: six percent less in a year. Mines and smelters are using less, and many homes and businesses have put up solar panels.

And when a company sells less, but still has to pay for its power stations and its debt, it has to charge more for every unit it sells.

That's why the electricity minister said in August 2026 that prices had risen far faster than inflation, and that the era of double-digit increases should end. And he had a message for municipalities that don't pay: you are not allowed to punish those who are paying, for those who are not paying.

Which brings us back to your bill.

The energy regulator, NERSA, decides how much Eskom may charge. Its job is to balance what Eskom needs to keep running with what customers can pay. Early in 2026, it found a mistake in its own numbers: fifty-four point seven billion rand that Eskom should have been allowed to recover. So the increase for this year jumped from about five percent to almost nine percent.

If you buy directly from Eskom, prices went up eight point seven six percent in April 2026. If you buy from your municipality, Eskom's price to municipalities went up nine point zero one percent in July. And Eskom's prices are set to rise again, by eight point eight three percent, in April 2027.

So what does that mean for Nomsa? If she spent one thousand rand a month on electricity, the same electricity now costs about one thousand and ninety rand. That's about ninety rand more every month, almost eleven hundred rand more a year, for exactly the same lights and the same kettle.

And since 2007? Electricity that cost one hundred rand then costs about a thousand rand now. Other things that cost one hundred rand then cost about two hundred and fifty.

Now look at what that does over a few years. Say Nomsa earns twelve thousand rand a month, and spends a thousand on electricity. That's just over eight percent of her pay. If electricity keeps rising nine percent a year, and her salary rises five percent a year, then in five years, electricity takes about ten percent of her pay. Same house. Same kettle. A bigger slice of her money.

So what does this mean for your money?

First: give electricity its own line in your budget, and give it a raise every year. When your municipality's increase comes in July, or Eskom's in April, add about nine percent to that line, before the price catches you by surprise.

Second: watch your units, not just your rand. Write down how many units five hundred rand buys you this month. Next July, check again. You'll see the increase in black and white.

Third: if your household income is low, ask your municipality whether you qualify for free basic electricity. Right now, it's often fifty units a month. The government's new pricing policy, approved by Cabinet in August 2026, proposes raising it to between two hundred and three hundred units for qualifying households, but that is still a proposal.

And fourth: remember that electricity is now one of the bills that grows fastest. When you negotiate a raise, plan a budget, or think about solar, count on it costing more next year than it does today.

The good news? Every unit you don't use is a unit you don't pay for, at next year's price too. In a future guide, we'll go through how prepaid tariffs work, and how to get more units for your money.

Let's recap.

Eskom didn't build in time, load shedding began in 2007, and two giant power stations went hundreds of billions over budget. The debt grew so big that the government stepped in with up to two hundred and fifty-four billion rand.

Today, load shedding has mostly stopped, and Eskom is making a profit again. But it's selling less, municipalities owe it more than a hundred and eleven billion rand, and your price is still rising almost nine percent a year.

So give electricity its own line in your budget, with a raise every year.
